Hopf Algebra on Vincular Permutation Patterns
Joscha Diehl †, Emanuele Verri †

Abstract
We introduce a new Hopf algebra that operates on pairs of finite interval partitions and permutations of equal length. This algebra captures vincular patterns , which involve specifying both the permutation patterns and the consecutive occurrence of values. Our motivation stems from linear functionals that encode the number of occurrences of these patterns, and we show that they behave well with respect to the operations of this Hopf algebra.



1
Introduction

Permutation patterns
are ubiquitous in discrete mathematics. Much effort is devoted to developing algorithms that count these patterns efficiently, see for example
[
6
]
and
[
7
]
.

They have also been successfully used in
time series analysis
in the popular work from
[
2
]
, where the authors introduced the concept of
permutation entropy
. For a discrete time series, consider only the order of the values. As an example, the time series

1 2 3 4 5 6

can be “reduced” to the permutation
134265\in\mathbf{S}_{6}
. Permutation entropy is based on specific permutation patterns, namely consecutive patterns. If we fix an order for the patterns, say 2, we observe

12

12

21

12

21

The frequencies of
12,21\in\mathbf{S}_{2}
are needed to compute the permutation entropy of order 2. In general, for the permutation entropy of order
n
, we would compute the frequencies of the elements of
\mathbf{S}_{n}
of consecutive patterns of length
n
.

On the other hand, many notable constructions on permutations have been introduced in
algebraic combinatorics
: the Malvenuto-Reutenauer Hopf algebra on permutations is the most celebrated example,
[
10
]
.

In
[
15
]
, the author introduces a Hopf algebra on permutations. Let
\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{m}
and
\tau\in\mathbf{S}_{n}
, then

\displaystyle\Delta_{\,\scriptsize\raisebox{1.50694pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}}(\sigma)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A,B\subset[m]\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\\
\\
A\cup B=[m]\end{subarray}}\mathbf{st}\left(\sigma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$}\right)\otimes\mathbf{st}\left(\sigma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{B}$}\right),

\displaystyle\sigma\square\tau\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sigma_{1}\cdots\sigma_{m}(\tau_{1}+m)\cdots(\tau_{n}+m).

where, for example

\displaystyle\Delta_{\,\scriptsize\raisebox{1.50694pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}}(21)=\mathsf{e}\otimes 21+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2}\cdot 1\otimes 1+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2}\cdot 1\otimes 21+21\otimes\mathsf{e}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2}\cdot 21\otimes 1+21\otimes 21,

\displaystyle 21\square 12=2134.

and it is there shown that
\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{per}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Q}[\mathbf{S}_{n}],\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}},\Delta_{\scriptsize\square})
is a
filtered
Hopf algebra. This construction relates to occurrences of permutation patterns. Denote with
\mathbf{S}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigcup_{n}\mathbf{S}_{n}
, the set of all permutations, and consider the family of linear functionals
(\textbf{pattern}(\sigma))_{\sigma\in\mathbf{S}}
, defined on basis elements,
\Lambda\in\mathbf{S}
as

\displaystyle\Big\langle\textbf{pattern}(\sigma),\Lambda\Big\rangle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\#\{A\subset[|\Lambda|]|\;\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma\},

i.e. the occurrences of
\sigma
as a
pattern
on
\Lambda
. We can endow
\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{S}}
, the set of all functions from
\mathbf{S}
to
\mathbb{Q}
, with a
\mathbb{Q}
-algebra structure using the pointwise product

\displaystyle\forall f,g\in\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{S}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\forall\sigma\in\mathbf{S}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\;\;(f+g)(\sigma)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=f(\sigma)+g(\sigma),\,(f\cdot g)(\sigma)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=f(\sigma)\cdot g(\sigma).

Then Vargas showed that

\displaystyle\left(\bigoplus_{n}\mathbb{Q}[\mathbf{S}_{n}],\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}\right)

\displaystyle\to\left(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{S}},\cdot\right),

\displaystyle\sigma

\displaystyle\mapsto\textbf{pattern}(\sigma)

is an (injective) algebra homomorpshism, i.e., for all
\Lambda\in\mathbf{S}

\displaystyle\Big\langle\textbf{pattern}(\sigma\;\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}\;\tau),\Lambda\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\textbf{pattern}(\sigma),\Lambda\Big\rangle\Big\langle\textbf{pattern}(\tau),\Lambda\Big\rangle.

Taking on a slightly different approach, we fix
\Lambda\in\mathbf{S}
, vary the pattern
\sigma
and define the family of functionals

\displaystyle\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda),\sigma\Big\rangle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\#\{A\subset[|\Lambda|]|\;\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma\},

and call
\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda)
the
signature
of the permutation
\Lambda
. The term “signature” is motivated by the following identity

\displaystyle\forall\sigma,\tau\in\mathbf{S}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\;\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda),\sigma\Big\rangle\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda),\tau\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda),\sigma\;\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}\;\tau\Big\rangle

(1)

which is reminiscent of the shuffle identity for the signature of a path
(
[
8
,
13
,
5
]
).
For example

\displaystyle\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),1\Big\rangle\cdot\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),1\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}\Big(\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_perm_132.png}}\Big),\raisebox{-2.15277pt}{\includegraphics[width,height]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_perm_1.png}}\Big\rangle\cdot\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}\Big(\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_perm_132.png}}\Big),\raisebox{-2.15277pt}{\includegraphics[width,height]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_perm_1.png}}\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=|\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3\}\}\times\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3\}\}|

\displaystyle=|\{\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_left.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_left.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_left.png}}\}\times\{\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_right.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_right.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_right}}\}|

\displaystyle=|\{(\{1\},\{1\}),(\{1\},\{2\}),(\{1\},\{3\}),(\{2\},\{1\}),(\{2\},\{2\}),(\{2\},\{3\}),

\displaystyle(\{3\},\{1\}),(\{3\},\{2\}),(\{3\},\{3\})\}|

\displaystyle=|\{\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_1.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_2.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_3.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_1.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_2.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_3.png}}

\displaystyle\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_1.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_2.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_3.png}}\}|

\displaystyle=|\{(\{1\},\{1\}),(\{2\},\{2\}),(\{3\},\{3\})\}|

\displaystyle+|\{(\{1\},\{2\}),(\{2\},\{1\}),(\{1\},\{3\}),(\{3\},\{1\})\}|

\displaystyle+|\{(\{2\},\{3\}),(\{3\},\{2\})\}|

\displaystyle=|\{\overbrace{\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_1.png}}}^{\langle 1\otimes 1,\Delta_{\scriptsize\,\raisebox{1.50694pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}}(1)\rangle=1},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_2.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_3.png}}\}|

\displaystyle+|\overbrace{\{\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_2.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_1.png}}}^{\langle 1\otimes 1,\Delta_{\scriptsize\,\raisebox{1.50694pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}}(12)\rangle=2},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_1_3.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_1.png}}\}|

\displaystyle+|\overbrace{\{\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_2_3.png}},\raisebox{-4.30554pt}{ \includegraphics[scale]{pictures/vargas_signature_example/Figure_3_2.png}}\}}^{\langle 1\otimes 1,\Delta_{\scriptsize\,\raisebox{1.50694pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}}(21)\rangle=2}|

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),1\Big\rangle+2\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),12\Big\rangle+2\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),21\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),1+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2}\,12+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2}\,21\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{PC}(132),1\,\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}\,1\Big\rangle.

This terminology is also motivated by an identity
similar to
Chen’s identity
(
[
9
, p.10]
)

\displaystyle\forall\Lambda,\Upsilon\in\mathbf{S}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\;\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda\square\Upsilon)=\mathsf{PC}(\Lambda)\square\mathsf{PC}(\Upsilon).

(2)

Inspired by the work of
[
2
]
and
[
15
]
, aim of this work is to generalize the

\Rightarrow

-Hopf algebra to encode more general patterns. Given a permutation
\Lambda
, we search for permutation patterns
\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{n_{k}}

where for all
j=1,\dots,k
,
n_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=0
, the values from
n_{j-1}+1
to
n_{j}
need to occur consecutively in time. These patterns are known in the literature as
vincular permutation patterns
. They seem to have been first introduced in
[
1
]
;
see also
[
3
]
using the more recent term “vincular pattern”.

As an example, Let
2
1

3
, be the pattern we search on
134265
. Then

426

425

325

426
and
425
are compatible with

2
1

3

while
325
is not. We encode this information as a
pair
:
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)
, where

\mathfrak{s}

is an
interval partition
of
[n]
, and
\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}
, a permutation of the same “size”. In this example, we have:

\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{}{{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=(\{\{1,2\},\{3\}\},213)
.

As an intermediate step, we introduce a new Hopf algebra on interval partitions

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Q}[\mathbf{StIP}_{n}],{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}},\Delta_{\bullet}\right)

where

\displaystyle\mathbf{StIP}_{n}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\;\text{is an interval partition of}\;[n]\}.

We define a corresponding family of “signatures”

\displaystyle\left(\mathsf{IPC}\left(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}\right)\right)_{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}}.

The terminology is again motivated by identities which hold for these functionals, analogous to
Equation

1
and
Equation

2
. Furthermore, we show that this Hopf algebra is isomorphic to a Hopf algebra on words, where the letters correspond to blocks of a partition. Finally, we “combine” our Hopf algebra on interval partitions with the superinfiltration

\Rightarrow

-Hopf algebra and define a new Hopf algebra on vincular permutation patterns,

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Q}[\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}],{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}},\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}}).

The
♥
product originates from our
♠
product on partitions and the

\Rightarrow

product on permutations, see
[
15
]
. The coproduct is also a “combination” of the other two. The Hopf algebra
\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}}
generalizes
\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{per}}
and
\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}}
as well. A correspondent family of signatures is also introduced.

2
Notation

–

We denote the natural numbers, including
0
,
with
\mathbb{N}

and the strictly positive natural numbers
with
\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
.

–

Let
A,B
be sets. If
A\cap B=\emptyset
, then we write
A\uplus B\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=A\cup B
. This notation comes in handy when we assume that the sets are disjoint.
With this notation,

\displaystyle|\biguplus_{i\in I}A_{i}|=\sum_{i\in I}|A_{i}|.

if only finitely many sets
A_{i}
are non-empty and
\forall i\in I\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}|A_{i}|<\infty
.

–

For
n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
we denote

\displaystyle[n]\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{1,\dots,n\}.

We set

\displaystyle[0]\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\emptyset.

–

We say that
\mathcal{I}
is a
(finite) partition

\mathcal{I}=\{\mathcal{I}_{1},...,\mathcal{I}_{I}\}

of a set
A

if the (finite) family
\mathcal{I}_{i},i\in I
, consists of non-empty, pairwise disjoint sets, and their union is
A
,

\bigcup_{i}\mathcal{I}_{i}=A
.
All partitions considered in this work are
finite interval partitions
of
finite subsets
of the positive integers. Let
A\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
, with
|A|<\infty
.
We say that
\mathcal{I}
is an
interval partition
of
A

if
\mathcal{I}
is a partition of
A
, whose blocks
\mathcal{I}_{j}
are intervals on
\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
. As an example, if
A=\{2,4,5\}
, then
\{\{4,5\},\{2\}\}
is an interval partition of
A
, while
\{\{2,4\},\{5\}\}
is not.
For a partition
\mathcal{I}
of a set
A
we also write

\displaystyle\bigcup\mathcal{I}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigcup_{i}\mathcal{I}_{i}=A,

for its ground-set.

–

The set

\displaystyle\mathbf{IP}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{X|X\;\text{is an interval partition of some finite subset of}\;\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}\}

contains “labeled” finite interval partition.

–

We also fix
A\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},A<\infty
and write

\displaystyle\mathbf{IP}(A)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{X|X\;\text{is an interval partition of}\;A\}

–

The subset

\displaystyle\mathbf{StIP}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\biguplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\subset\mathbf{IP}

where
\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{A|A\;\text{is an interval partition of}\;[n]\}
,
contains “unlabeled” or
standardized
interval partitions. Notice that
\mathbf{IP}(\emptyset)=\{\emptyset\}
, i.e., the unique partition for the empty set
\emptyset
is the empty set itself, which means

\displaystyle\mathbf{StIP}_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\emptyset\}.

Also, we have:

\displaystyle\mathbf{StIP}=\biguplus_{\ell\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{NB}_{\ell}

where

\displaystyle\mathbf{NB}_{\ell}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}|\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{\ell}\}\}

i.e., all standardized partitions having
\ell
blocks.

–

We use gothic letters to denote elements of
\mathbf{StIP}
, for example
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}
. We use capital calligraphical letters when we consider any element of
\mathbf{IP}
, for example
\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}
.

–

We define a partial order relation on
\mathbf{IP}
, as follows

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\leq\mathcal{J}\iff\bigcup\mathcal{I}=\bigcup\mathcal{J}\;\land\;\forall j\in J\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\exists i\in I\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathcal{I}_{i}\subset\mathcal{J}_{j}.

If
I
and
J
are not comparable, we write
I\perp J
.
As an example:
\{\{2\},\{3\},\{1\}\}\leq\{\{2,3\},\{1\}\}
, while
\{\{2\},\{3\},\{1\}\}\perp\{\{5\},\{3\},\{4\}\}
and
\{\{1,2\},\{3\}\}\perp\{\{1\},\{2,3\}\}
.

–

We denote with
\mathbf{S}_{n}
the symmetric group of order
n
,

\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{f|\;f\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}[n]\to[n]\;\text{is a bijection}\}.

Let
\mathbf{S}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigcup_{n}\mathbf{S}_{n}
denote the set of all permutations. Notice that
\mathbf{S}_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{f|f\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\,\emptyset\to\emptyset\}
contains the unique empty permutation. We denote elements of
\mathbf{S}
, with Greek letters, for example,
\sigma\in\mathbf{S}
. We use one-line notation, for example,

\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{2}=\{12,21\}.

–

Let
A
denote a set which we call
alphabet
. We call its elements
letters
. Denote with
A^{*}
the set of words on the alphabet, i.e. finite sequences of elements of
A
. If
A
is a totally ordered set, define the
standardization
of a word
w\in A^{*}
as the relative order of the letters which appear in
w
. If a letter appears more than once, we order them from left to right. For example, if
A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{N}
with the usual order

\displaystyle\mathbf{st}\left(234121\right)=356142.

Permutations written in one-line notation can be seen as (particular) words on positive integers. When we restrict
\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}
to a subset
A\subset[n]
, with
|A|=k
, we can standardize the subword to get an element of
\mathbf{S}_{k}
. As an example

\displaystyle\mathbf{st}\left(645123\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{\{2,4,5\}}$}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathbf{st}\left(423\right)=312.

–

If
\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}
, then
|\sigma|\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=n
. Analogously, if
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}_{n}
, then
|\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}|\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=n
.

3
Finite interval partitions

3.1
Auxiliary operations

Before introducing the algebraic operations, we need some auxiliary operations. Let
A
be a finite subset of
\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
. The following operation yields the coarsest interval partition of
A
.

Definition 3.1

(Cliques)
.

\displaystyle\mathbf{cliques}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\{A|A\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},|A|<\infty\}

\displaystyle\to\mathbf{IP}

\displaystyle A

\displaystyle\mapsto\{[x]_{\sim\langle\mathsf{Succ}_{A}\rangle}|x\in A\}

where
(x,y)\in\mathsf{Succ}_{A}\subset A\times A\iff y=x+1
and
\langle\mathsf{Succ}_{A}\rangle
is the equivalence relation generated by
\mathsf{Succ}_{A}
.

Example 3.2
.

\displaystyle\mathbf{cliques}(\{2,4,5,6\})

\displaystyle=\{\{2\},\{4,5,6\}\}

\displaystyle\mathbf{cliques}(\emptyset)

\displaystyle=\emptyset.

Remark 3.3
.

Let
\mathcal{I}
be any partition of
A
, then

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\text{ is an interval partition of $A$ }\Leftrightarrow\mathcal{I}\leq\mathbf{cliques}(A).

Now fix an interval partition
\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}
and a finite subset of positive integers,
A\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
. We define an interval partition of
A\cap\bigcup\mathcal{I}
as follows.

Definition 3.4

(Cliques of
A
through
\mathcal{I}
)
.

Let
\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}
and
A\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},A<\infty
.

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(A)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\mathcal{I}_{j}\cap c|\;c\in\mathbf{cliques}(A),j\in J\}\setminus\{\emptyset\}.

Remark 3.5
.

Since the intersection of two intervals is again an interval,
\mathcal{I}(A)
is a set of intervals. These intervals are pairwise disjoint since
\mathcal{I}
and
\mathbf{cliques}(A)
are partitions and this implies that
\mathcal{I}_{i}\cap c
and
\mathcal{I}_{j}\cap c^{\prime}
are also pairwise disjoint. We clearly have
\bigcup\mathcal{I}(A)=A\cap\bigcup\mathcal{I}
. Therefore, by
Remark

3.3
, one has

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(A)

\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{cliques}(A\cap\bigcup\mathcal{I}).

Example 3.6
.

For
\mathcal{I}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{2,3,4\}\}
and
A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{2,4,5\}

we have

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(A)=\{\{2\},\{4\}\}.

If
\mathcal{I}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{2,3\},\{4,5\},\{6,7\},\{8\}\}
and
A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{2,4,5,6\}

we have

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(A)=\{\{2\},\{4,5\},\{6\}\}<\{\{2\},\{4,5,6\}\}=\mathbf{cliques}(A\cap\bigcup\mathcal{I}).

In case
A=\emptyset

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(A)=\emptyset.

Finally, we can convert elements of
\mathbf{IP}
, into elements of
\mathbf{StIP}
as follows.

Definition 3.7

(Standardization of a partition)
.

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbf{IP}\to\mathbf{StIP}

Let
i_{1},\dots,i_{\ell_{1}},\dots,i_{\ell_{2}},\dots,i_{\ell_{k}}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},
where
k\in\mathbb{N}
, such that

\displaystyle i_{1}\prec\cdots\prec i_{\ell_{1}}<i_{\ell_{1}+1}\prec\cdots\prec i_{\ell_{2}}<\cdots<i_{\ell_{k-1}+1}\prec\cdots\prec i_{\ell_{k}}

where
i\prec j\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\iff j-i=1
. In other words, we consider an interval partition with
k
blocks. Then define

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}\left(\left\{\{i_{1},...,i_{\ell_{1}}\},\{i_{\ell_{1}+1},...,i_{\ell_{2}}\},...,\{i_{\ell_{k-1}+1},...,i_{\ell_{k}}\}\right\}\right)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{1,...,\ell_{1}\},\{\ell_{1}+1,...,\ell_{2}\},...,\{\ell_{k-1}+1,...,\ell_{k}\}\}

with

\displaystyle 1\prec\cdots\prec\ell_{1}\prec\ell_{1}+1\prec\cdots\prec\ell_{2}\prec\cdots\prec\ell_{k-1}+1\prec\cdots\prec\ell_{k}.

Example 3.8
.

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}(\{\{2\},\{4,5\},\{6\}\})=\{\{1\},\{2,3\},\{4\}\}

Remark 3.9
.

Let
\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}
. We can turn
A\subset\bigcup\mathcal{I}
, into a standardized interval partition, namely

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}(A)).

Example 3.10
.

If
\mathcal{I}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{2,3\},\{4,5\},\{6,7\},\{8\}\}
and
A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{2,4,5,6\}
, we have

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}(A))

\displaystyle=\{\{1\},\{2,3\},\{4\}\}.

3.1.1
Gluing partitions

We now introduce a binary operation on interval partitions.

Definition 3.11

(Gluing partitions)
.

Let
\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}
.
First define the relation

\displaystyle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\subset(\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J})\times(\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J})

\displaystyle(E,F)\in R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\iff E\cap F\neq\emptyset.

Then define the binary operation as

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left\{\bigcup_{X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X\Bigg|\;T\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}\right\},

where
\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle
is the smallest equivalence relation which contains
R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}
.

Example 3.12
.

Let
\mathcal{I}=\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3,4\},\{5,6,7\}\}
and
\mathcal{J}=\{\{2,3\},\{4,5\}\}
. Then

\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}=\{\{1\},\{2,3,4,5,6,7\}\}.

We visualize
R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}
in the following picture

\mathcal{I}=
\{1\}
\{2\}
\{3,4\}
\{5,6,7\}
\{4,5\}
\{2,3\}
\mathcal{J}=

We now state several lemmas that clarify the behavior of the gluing operation.

Lemma 3.13
.

Let
\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}
. Then

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}\left(\bigcup\mathcal{I}\cup\bigcup\mathcal{J}\right).

In particular
\forall\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP},\;\;\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}.

Proof.

Let
T\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}
and consider its equivalence class

\displaystyle[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}.

From the definition of
\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle
it follows that we can write

\displaystyle[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}=\{X_{1},...,X_{n}\}\;\text{where}\;X_{i}\in\mathcal{I}\lor X_{i}\in\mathcal{J}

for some positive integer
n
, where
\forall i\in\{1,...,n-1\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}X_{i}\cap X_{i+1}\neq\emptyset
.
Obviously, the union of two intersecting intervals is again an interval.
It then follows by induction that

\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}

is an interval. It remains to show that

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}=\left\{\bigcup_{X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X\Bigg|\;T\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}\right\}

is a partition of
\bigcup\mathcal{I}\cup\bigcup\mathcal{J}
. Clearly

\displaystyle\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}}\bigcup_{X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X=\bigcup\mathcal{I}\cup\bigcup\mathcal{J}.

Since

\displaystyle\left\{[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}\Bigg|\;T\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}\right\}

is a partition of the blocks of
\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}
, we have that

\displaystyle\forall T\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{J}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}\neq\emptyset.

and therefore
\bigcup_{X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X\neq\emptyset
. Now let

\displaystyle\bigcup_{X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X\cap\bigcup_{X\in[S]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X\neq\emptyset.

This means
\exists X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}
and
\exists Y\in[S]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}
such that
X\cap Y\neq\emptyset
. Therefore
[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}=[S]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}
, which means

\displaystyle\bigcup_{X\in[T]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X=\bigcup_{X\in[S]_{\sim\langle R_{\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}}\rangle}}X.

∎

This operation is associative.

Lemma 3.14
.

Let
\mathcal{I},\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}
. Then

\displaystyle(\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}).

For a proof of this result, see
Lemma

A.10
, which can be seen as an instance of a more general phenomenon, we refer to
Appendix

A
.

Lemma 3.15
.

Let
A,A^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
be finite subsets. Let
\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}(A)
and
\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})
. If

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\leq\mathcal{J}\;\text{and}\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\leq\mathcal{J}^{\prime},

then

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\leq\mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}.

Proof.

Let
z\in\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}
. Then

\displaystyle z=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}X_{i},

where
\forall i\in\{1,...,m-1\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}X_{i}\cap X_{i+1}\neq\emptyset
and
X_{i}\in\mathcal{I}
or
X_{i}\in\mathcal{I}^{\prime}
. From the hypothesis, we know that

\displaystyle\forall i\in\{1,...,m\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\exists Y_{i}\in\mathcal{J}\cup\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}X_{i}\subset Y_{i}.

Now since

\displaystyle\forall i\in\{1,...,m-1\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Y_{i}\cap Y_{i+1}\supset X_{i}\cap X_{i+1}\neq\emptyset,

We have that
\exists w\in\mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}
such that

z\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}Y_{i}\subset w
and we are done.
∎

Corollary 3.16
.

Let
\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}
,
A,A^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},|A|,|A^{\prime}|<\infty
. Then

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(A)\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}(A^{\prime})\leq\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}=\mathcal{Z}^{\prime}=\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime})
,
\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{I}(A)
and
\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{J}(A)
. We just need to show that
\mathcal{W}\leq\mathcal{W}^{\prime}
and
\mathcal{Z}\leq\mathcal{Z}^{\prime}
hold. We can then apply
Lemma

3.15
: it follows immediately from the definition of
\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}
that
\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{Z}^{\prime}=\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime})\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime})=\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime})
. First, for any
c\in\mathbf{cliques}(A)

and any
x\in c

\displaystyle c=[x]_{\sim\langle\mathsf{Succ}_{A}\rangle}\subset[x]_{\sim\langle\mathsf{Succ}_{A\cup A^{\prime}}\rangle}\in\mathbf{cliques}(A\cup A^{\prime}).

Let
X\in\mathcal{I}(A)
.
Claim: there is a
Y\in\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime})

with

\displaystyle X\subset Y.

Indeed, we can write
X=c\cap\mathcal{I}_{j}
for some
c\in\mathbf{cliques}(A),\mathcal{I}_{j}\in\mathcal{I}
.
Then, for any
x\in c
,

\displaystyle X=(c\cap\mathcal{I}_{j})\subset([x]_{\sim\langle\mathsf{Succ}_{A\cup A^{\prime}}\rangle}\cap\mathcal{I}_{j})=\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Y\in\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime}).

Analogously, for every
X\in\mathcal{I}(A^{\prime})

there is a
Y\in\mathcal{I}(A\cup A^{\prime})
with
X\subset Y
.
∎

Lemma 3.17
.

Let
\mathcal{I},\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}
. Consider

\displaystyle\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}.

Then

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\leq\mathcal{J}(\bigcup\mathcal{I})\;\text{and}\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\leq\mathcal{J}(\bigcup\mathcal{I}^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let
z\in\mathcal{J}
, then

\displaystyle z=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}

where
\forall i\in\{1,...,n-1\}
,
X_{i}\cap X_{i+1}\neq\emptyset
and
X_{i}\in\mathcal{I}
or
X_{i}\in\mathcal{I}^{\prime}
.
Now recall that

\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\bigcup\mathcal{I})

\displaystyle=\{c\cap\mathcal{J}_{i}|c\in\mathbf{cliques}(\bigcup\mathcal{I}),i\in I\}\setminus\{\emptyset\},

\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\bigcup\mathcal{I}^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=\{c\cap\mathcal{J}_{i}|c\in\mathbf{cliques}(\bigcup\mathcal{I}^{\prime}),i\in I\}\setminus\{\emptyset\}.

Let
w\in\mathcal{I}
, then obviously there exists a
z\in\mathcal{J}
such that
w\subset z
. Also by definition of
\mathbf{cliques}(\bigcup\mathcal{I})
, we know that
\mathcal{I}\leq\mathbf{cliques}(\bigcup\mathcal{I})
and therefore
\exists c\in\mathbf{cliques}(\bigcup\mathcal{I})
such that
w\subset c
. Therefore
w\subset z\cap c
which means that
\mathcal{I}\leq\mathcal{J}(\bigcup\mathcal{I})
. Analogously one shows that
\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\leq\mathcal{J}(\bigcup\mathcal{I}^{\prime})
.
∎

(3)

3.2.1
Products, coproducts

We now define a (non-commutative) product on interval partitions.

Definition 3.19
.

Let
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{m}\},\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}_{n}\}\in\mathbf{StIP}
. Then define

\displaystyle\bullet\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}}\to\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}}

\displaystyle\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{m},\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}_{n}\}

where for
i=1,...,n
,
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=|\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}|+\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}_{i}
. And extend linearly.

.

\displaystyle\{\{1,2\}\}\bullet\{\{1\},\{2\}\}=\{\{1,2\},\{3\},\{4\}\}

To denote elements of
\mathbf{StIP}
, we will also simply write

\displaystyle\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\bullet\Box\>\Box\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{1,2\}\}\bullet\{\{1\},\{2\}\}=\{\{1,2\},\{3\},\{4\}\}=\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\;\Box{}\;\Box

and
\mathsf{e}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\emptyset
.

.

The

Proof.

The proof is immediate and is left to the reader.

We now define a coproduct which is based on the gluing operation.

Definition 3.22
.

Let
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}
.

We define a (cocommutative) coproduct as follows

\displaystyle\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})

and extend linearly. Recall that from
Lemma

3.17
, it follows that
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}
implies that
\mathcal{I}\leq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}(A)
and
\mathcal{I}\leq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}(A^{\prime})
.

\displaystyle+2\ \Box\ \Box\otimes\Box+\Box\ \Box\otimes\Box\ \Box

Remark 3.24

(Shuffle coproduct)
.

Notice that
\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}
has a “co-shuffle part”. Indeed

\displaystyle\Delta_{\shuffle}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{A\uplus A^{\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}).

is a shuffle coproduct. As an example

\displaystyle\Delta_{\shuffle}(\ \Box\ \Box\ )

\displaystyle=\mathsf{e}\otimes\Box\ \Box+\Box\ \Box\otimes\mathsf{e}+2\ \Box\otimes\Box\,.

More precisely,
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}},\Delta_{\shuffle})
is isomorphic to a coalgebra on words, where letters are positive integers, see
Remark

3.33
. For example

\displaystyle\Delta_{\shuffle,\,\textbf{words}}(1\text{♠}1)=\mathsf{e}\otimes 1\text{♠}1+1\text{♠}1\otimes\mathsf{e}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2}\,1\otimes 1,

where
♠
denotes the concatenation of words and
\Delta_{\shuffle,\textbf{words}}
is the usual shuffle coproduct on words.

Proposition 3.25
.

The coproduct
\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}
is coassociative.

We first need the following lemma.

Lemma 3.26
.

Let
\mathcal{W},\mathcal{Z}\in\mathbf{IP}
such that
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{W})=\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{Z})
. Then

\displaystyle=\bigcup_{A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\mathcal{W}}\{(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}),\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}))|\;\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime}),\;\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\mathcal{W}\}

\displaystyle\bigcup_{B\cup B^{\prime}=\bigcup\mathcal{Z}}\{(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J}),\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}))|\;\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}(B),\;\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(B^{\prime}),\;\mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}=\mathcal{Z}\}.

In particular,
\forall\mathcal{W}\in\mathbf{IP}

\displaystyle\bigcup_{A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\mathcal{W}}\{(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}),\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}))|\;\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime}),\;\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\mathcal{W}\}

\displaystyle=\bigcup_{B\cup B^{\prime}=\bigcup\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{W})_{j}}\{(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J}),\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}))|\;\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}(B),\;\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(B^{\prime}),\;\mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}=\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{W})\}.

Proof.

We recall the notation used in
Definition

3.7

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}

\displaystyle=\{\{w_{1},...,w_{\ell_{1}}\},\{w_{\ell_{1}+1},...,w_{\ell_{2}}\},...,\{w_{\ell_{k-1}+1},...,w_{\ell_{k}}\}\}

\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}

\displaystyle=\{\{z_{1},...,z_{\ell_{1}}\},\{z_{\ell_{1}+1},...,z_{\ell_{2}}\},...,\{z_{\ell_{k-1}+1},...,z_{\ell_{k}}\}\}

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{W})

\displaystyle=\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{Z})=\{\{1,...,\ell_{1}\},\{\ell_{1}+1,...,\ell_{2}\},...,\{\ell_{k-1}+1,...,\ell_{k}\}\}.

Consider the map

\displaystyle f\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\bigcup\mathcal{W}

\displaystyle\to\bigcup\mathcal{Z}

\displaystyle w_{j}

\displaystyle\mapsto z_{j}

Now, let
A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\mathcal{W}
, such that
\exists\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\mathcal{W}
. We can write

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}=\{\{w_{h_{1}},\dots,w_{h_{2}}\},\{w_{h_{2}+1},\dots,w_{h_{3}}\},\dots,\{w_{h_{l-1}+1},\dots,w_{h_{l}}\}\}

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\{\{w_{s_{1}},\dots,w_{s_{2}}\},\{w_{s_{2}+1},\dots,w_{s_{3}}\},\dots,\{w_{s_{m-1}+1},\dots,w_{s_{m}}\}\}.

where
(h_{i})
and
(s_{i})
are subsequences of
(\ell_{i})
.
Then

\displaystyle f(\mathcal{I})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{f(w_{h_{1}}),\dots,f(w_{h_{2}})\},\{f(w_{h_{2}+1}),\dots,f(w_{h_{3}})\},\dots,\{f(w_{h_{l-1}+1}),\dots,f(w_{h_{l}})\}\}

\displaystyle=\{\{z_{h_{1}},\dots,z_{h_{2}}\},\{z_{h_{2}+1},\dots,z_{h_{3}}\},\dots,\{z_{h_{l-1}+1},\dots,z_{h_{l}}\}\},

\displaystyle f(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\{f(w_{s_{1}}),\dots,f(w_{s_{2}})\},\{f(w_{s_{2}+1}),\dots,f(w_{s_{3}})\},\dots,\{f(w_{s_{m-1}+1}),\dots,f(w_{s_{m}})\}\}

\displaystyle=\{\{z_{s_{1}},\dots,z_{s_{2}}\},\{z_{s_{2}+1},\dots,z_{s_{3}}\},\dots,\{z_{s_{m-1}+1},\dots,z_{s_{m}}\}\}.

Now, we clearly have

\displaystyle A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\mathcal{W}\iff f(A)\cup f(A^{\prime})=\bigcup\mathcal{Z}

and also

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\mathcal{W}\iff f(\mathcal{I})\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}f(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\mathcal{Z}.

since

\displaystyle\{w_{h_{i-1}+1},\dots,w_{h_{i}}\}\cap\{w_{s_{j-1}+1},\dots,w_{s_{j}}\}\neq\emptyset\iff\{z_{h_{i-1}+1},\dots,z_{h_{i}}\}\cap\{z_{s_{j-1}+1},\dots,z_{s_{j}}\}\neq\emptyset.

Moreover

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\mathbf{std}(\{\{w_{h_{1}},\dots,w_{h_{2}}\},\{w_{h_{2}+1},\dots,w_{h_{3}}\},\dots,\{w_{h_{l-1}+1},\dots,w_{h_{l}}\}\})

\displaystyle=\mathbf{std}(\{\{z_{h_{1}},\dots,z_{h_{2}}\},\{z_{h_{2}+1},\dots,z_{h_{3}}\},\dots,\{z_{h_{l-1}+1},\dots,z_{h_{l}}\}\})=\mathbf{std}(f(\mathcal{I})).

∎

Proof of
Proposition

3.25
.

Let
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}
. Since the gluing operation is associative, see
Lemma

3.14
, the expression

\displaystyle\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}\cup A^{\prime\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime}),\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime\prime})\\
\\
\ {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime})

is well-defined.
We have

\displaystyle\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}\cup A^{\prime\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime}),\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime\prime})\\
\\
\ \mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=\sum_{B\cup A^{\prime\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}(B),\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime\prime})\\
\\
\ \mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}\Bigg(\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=B}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\ \mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\mathcal{J}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\Bigg)\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=^{\hskip-19.91684pt\tiny\raisebox{6.80565pt}{\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap\lx@tilde refnum}{lemma:coassociativity_intpart}}}}\sum_{B\cup A^{\prime\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}(B),\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime\prime})\\
\\
\ \mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}

\displaystyle\Bigg(\sum_{X\cup Y=\cup_{i}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J})_{i}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(X),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(Y)\\
\\
\ \mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J})\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\Bigg)\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=(\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}).

Similarly, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}\cup A^{\prime\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime}),\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime\prime})\\
\\
\ \mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\otimes\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}})\circ\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}).

∎

Remark 3.27
.

The dual associative product is given by

\mathfrak{s}

♠

\mathfrak{t}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{\mathfrak{g}\in\mathbf{StIP}}\langle\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\otimes\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\Delta_{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$})\rangle\,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathfrak{g}\in\mathbf{StIP}}\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}_{i}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\;\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}\end{subarray}}\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}

\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\;\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}.

.
