4.1.2
Bialgebras on vincular permutations

We have an analogous result to
Theorem

3.30
.

Theorem 4.13

(Bialgebras on vincular permutations)
.

The following holds:

–

(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}},\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$},\Delta_{{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}},u^{\prime},\varepsilon^{\prime})
is a bialgebra,

–

(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}},{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}},\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}},u^{\prime},\varepsilon^{\prime})
is a connected filtered Hopf algebra (whith grading defined in
Equation

8
),

where
u^{\prime}
denotes the unit map and
\varepsilon^{\prime}
the counit map.

Proof.

Let
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\in\mathbf{StIP}_{m}\times\mathbf{S}_{m}
and
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)\in\mathbf{StIP}_{m}\times\mathbf{S}_{m}
. Recall that

\displaystyle\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}_{m},\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}_{n}\}

where for
i=1,...,n
,
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=|\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}|+\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}_{i}
. We also write
\tau_{m}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=(\tau_{1}+m)\cdots(\tau_{n}+m)
.
First, we have that

\displaystyle\Delta_{{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau))

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=[m+n]}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}),\mathbf{st}((\sigma\square\tau)|_{A}))\otimes(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}),\mathbf{st}((\sigma\square\tau)|_{A^{\prime}})).

is equal to

\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A_{1}\cup A_{1}^{\prime}=\{1,...,m\}\\
\\
A_{2}\cup A_{2}^{\prime}=\{m+1,...,m+n\}\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}_{1}\in\mathbf{IP}(A_{1}),\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A_{1}^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{I}_{2}\in\mathbf{IP}(A_{2}),\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A_{2}^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{I}_{1}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\;\mathcal{I}_{2}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}^{\prime}\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}_{1}),\mathbf{st}(\sigma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A_{1}}$}))\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$}(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}_{2}),\mathbf{st}(\tau_{m}\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A_{2}}$}))

\displaystyle\otimes(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\prime}),\mathbf{st}(\sigma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A_{1}^{\prime}}$}))\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$}(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\prime}),\mathbf{st}(\tau_{m}\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A_{2}^{\prime}}$}))

which, using arguments similar to the proof of
Theorem

3.30
, can be shown to be equal to

\displaystyle\Delta_{{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma))\;\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$}\;\Delta_{{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau))

\displaystyle=\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}),\mathbf{st}(\sigma|_{A}))\otimes(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}),\mathbf{st}(\sigma|_{A^{\prime}}))

\displaystyle\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$}\sum_{B\cup B^{\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}(B),\;\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(B^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathcal{J}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J}),\mathbf{st}(\tau|_{B}))\otimes(\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}),\mathbf{st}(\tau|_{B^{\prime}})).

∎

We can embed the Hopf algebra of the previous section.

Proposition 4.14

(Embedding of partitions)
.

The map

\displaystyle(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}},{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}},\Delta_{\bullet})

\displaystyle\to(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}},{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}},\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}})

\displaystyle\psi\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup\mathfrak{s}|}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma).

is an injective Hopf homomorphism.

We will use the following simple observation.

Lemma 4.15
.

Let
A,A^{\prime}\subset[n]
.
Then

\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{n}

\displaystyle=\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{|A|}\\
\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathbf{S}_{|A^{\prime}|}\end{subarray}}\{\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}|\ \mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-5.11108pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma,\ \mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-5.11108pt}{$|_{A^{\prime}}$})=\sigma^{\prime}\},

where the union is over disjoint, but possibly empty, sets.

Proof.

If
\sigma=\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$})=\hat{\sigma}
,

\sigma^{\prime}=\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A^{\prime}}$})=\hat{\sigma}^{\prime}
,
then
\sigma=\hat{\sigma},\sigma^{\prime}=\hat{\sigma}^{\prime}
, which proves disjointness
of the sets.
Finally, taking for
\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}
,

\sigma\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$}),\sigma^{\prime}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A^{\prime}}$})
, proves
the claimed identity.
∎

Proof of
Proposition

4.14
.

Let
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}_{k}
and
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\in\mathbf{StIP}_{k^{\prime}}
. We have

\displaystyle\psi(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\ {{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}\ \resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$})=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}}(\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\gamma)

and

\displaystyle\psi(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}){\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}\psi(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{k}\\
\tau\in\mathbf{S}_{k^{\prime}}\end{subarray}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]\\
|A|=k,|A^{\prime}|=k^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}\\
\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma,\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{A^{\prime}}$})=\tau\end{subarray}}(\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]\\
|A|=k,|A^{\prime}|=k^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{k},\tau\in\mathbf{S}_{k^{\prime}}\\
\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma,\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{A^{\prime}}$})=\tau\end{subarray}}(\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\gamma)

\displaystyle=^{\hskip-19.91684pt\tiny\raisebox{6.80565pt}{\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap\lx@tilde refnum}{lemma:partition_embedding}}}}\psi(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$})

While for the coalgebra part

\displaystyle(\psi\otimes\psi)\circ(\Delta_{\bullet}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}))=(\psi\otimes\psi)\circ(\sum_{\mathfrak{a}\bullet\mathfrak{b}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$}\otimes\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathfrak{a}\bullet\mathfrak{b}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{a}_{j}|}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$},\alpha)\otimes\sum_{\beta\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{b}_{j}|}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$},\beta)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathfrak{a}\bullet\mathfrak{b}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{a}_{j}|}}\sum_{\beta\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{b}_{j}|}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$},\alpha)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$},\beta)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j}|}}\sum_{\mathfrak{a}\bullet\mathfrak{b}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{a}_{j}|}}\sum_{\beta\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{b}_{j}|}}\sum_{\alpha\;\square\;\beta=\sigma}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$},\alpha)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$},\beta).

and

\displaystyle\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}}\circ\psi(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j}|}}\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma))

\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j}|}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\bullet\mathfrak{b}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\\
\alpha\square\beta=\sigma\\
\alpha\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{a}_{j}|},\beta\in\mathbf{S}_{|\cup_{j}\mathfrak{b}_{j}|}\end{subarray}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$},\alpha)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$},\beta).

∎

Proposition 4.16

(Embedding of permutations)
.

The Hopf algebra
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{per}},\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}},\Delta_{\scriptsize\square})
which appears in
[
15
]
can be embedded in
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}},{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}},\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}})
. Indeed the map

\displaystyle\phi\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\sigma

\displaystyle\mapsto(\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\sigma|\}\},\sigma),

where
\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\sigma|\}\}
is the singletons’ partition, is an injective Hopf homomorphism.

For the proof, we need two lemmas.

Lemma 4.17
.

Let
A,A^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1},|A|,|A^{\prime}|<\infty
and let
\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})
be the singletons’ partitions of
A
and
A^{\prime}
respectively. Then

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A\cup A^{\prime})

is the singletons’ partition of
A\cup A^{\prime}
.

Proof.

It follows immediately from the definition of
\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}
.
∎

Lemma 4.18
.

Let
n\in\mathbb{N}
. Then

\displaystyle\Big|\biguplus_{A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]}\{\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\mid\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|A|\},\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|A^{\prime}|\},

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\{\{1\},...,\{n\}\}\}\Big|

\displaystyle=\Big|\{A,A^{\prime}\subset[n]|A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]\}\Big|.

Proof.

It follows immediately, since for
A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]

\displaystyle|\{\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})|\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|A|\},\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|A^{\prime}|\},

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\{\{1\},...,\{n\}\}\}|

\displaystyle=1.

∎

Proof of
Proposition

4.16
.

Let
\sigma,\tau\in\mathbf{S}
.

\displaystyle\phi(\sigma){\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}\phi(\tau)

\displaystyle=\sum_{(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)}\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}}\;\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\sigma|\}\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\tau|\}\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma,\mathbf{st}(\gamma\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{A^{\prime}}$})=\tau}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)

\displaystyle=^{\hskip-19.91684pt\tiny\raisebox{6.80565pt}{\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap\lx@tilde refnum}{lemma:emb_perm2}}}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}}\sum_{A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}(A),\;\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}(A^{\prime})\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\sigma|\}\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime})=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\tau|\}\\
\\
\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime}=\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq n\}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\mathbf{st}(\gamma|_{A})=\sigma,\;\mathbf{st}(\gamma|_{A^{\prime}})=\tau}(\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq n\},\gamma)

\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbf{S}_{n}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup A^{\prime}=[n]\\
\\
\mathbf{st}(\gamma|_{A})=\sigma,\;\mathbf{st}(\gamma|_{A^{\prime}})=\tau\end{subarray}}(\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq n\},\gamma)

\displaystyle=\phi(\sigma\;\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}}\;\tau).

While for the coalgebra part

\displaystyle\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}}(\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\sigma|\},\sigma))=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\alpha|+|\beta|=|\sigma|\\
\alpha\square\beta=\sigma\end{subarray}}(\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\alpha|\},\alpha)\otimes(\{\{i\}|1\leq i\leq|\beta|\},\beta)

\displaystyle=\phi\otimes\phi\circ\Delta_{\square}(\sigma).

∎

4.2
Signature for vincular permutation patterns

In an analogous fashion to
Definition

3.34
, define, for
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}

\displaystyle\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\Big\rangle

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\#\{A\subset[N]|\;\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(A))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma\}.

and extend linearly to
\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}}
. These patterns are known in the literature as
vincular patterns
. They appear in
[
1
]
.

4.2.1
Character property and Chen’s identity

Again, we have analogous results to
Theorem

3.37
and
Theorem

3.46
.

Theorem 4.19

(Character property)
.

Let
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)\in\mathbf{StIP}_{N}\times\mathbf{S}_{N}
, with
N\in\mathbb{N}
. Then
\forall(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}
,

\displaystyle\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\Big\rangle\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma){\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)\Big\rangle.

Proof.

Using arguments analogous to the proof of
Theorem

3.37
, we have

\displaystyle|\{A,B\subset[N]|\;\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(A))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(B))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma,\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{B}$})=\tau\}|

\displaystyle=|\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma,C)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}\times 2^{N}\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(C))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}\\
\\
\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{C}$})=\gamma\end{subarray}}\{A,B\subset[N]\;|A\cup B=C,\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(A))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(B))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(A)_{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(B)_{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$}})=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$})=\sigma,\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{B}$})=\tau,\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{C}$})=\gamma\}|

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma,C)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}\times 2^{N}\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(C))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}\\
\\
\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{C}$})=\gamma\end{subarray}}\langle{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\rangle

\displaystyle=\sum_{(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in 2^{N}\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(C))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}\\
\\
\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{C}$})=\gamma\end{subarray}}\langle{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\rangle

\displaystyle=\sum_{(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}}\langle{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\rangle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}C\in 2^{N}\\
\\
\mathbf{std}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}(C))\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$}\\
\\
\mathbf{st}(\Lambda\,\raisebox{-3.98611pt}{$|_{C}$})=\gamma\end{subarray}}1

\displaystyle=\sum_{(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}}\langle{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\rangle\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),\sum_{(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}}\langle{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\otimes(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\rangle(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{g}$},\gamma)\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma){\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{t}$},\tau)\Big\rangle.

∎

Theorem 4.20

(Chen’s identity)
.

Let
N_{1},N_{2}\in\mathbb{N}
and let
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)\in\mathbf{StIP}_{N_{1}}\times\mathbf{S}_{N_{1}}
and
(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$},M)\in\mathbf{StIP}_{N_{2}}\times\mathbf{S}_{N_{2}}
, then
\forall(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{StIP}_{n}\times\mathbf{S}_{n}

\displaystyle\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}\Big((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)\resizebox{}{39322}{$\blacksquare$}(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$},M)\Big),(\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma)\Big\rangle

\displaystyle=\Big\langle\mathsf{GPC}\Big((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},\Lambda)\Big)\otimes\mathsf{GPC}\Big((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$},M)\Big),\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}}((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},\sigma))\Big\rangle

Proof.

Recall that
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}=\{\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}_{p},\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}^{\prime}_{1},...,\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}_{q}^{\prime}\}
, where
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}^{\prime}_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}_{i}+|\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}|
, where
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}^{\prime}_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}_{i}+|\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}|
, and
\sigma\square\tau=\sigma_{1}\cdots\sigma_{m}(\tau_{1}+m)\cdots(\tau_{n}+m)
. We have

\displaystyle|\{A\subset[N_{1}+N_{2}]|\;\mathbf{std}\left((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$})(A)\right)\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$},(\Lambda\square M)\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A}$}=\sigma\}|

\displaystyle=|\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathfrak{a}\bullet\mathfrak{b}=\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{s}$}\\
\\
\alpha\square\beta=\sigma\\
\\
\alpha\in\mathbf{S}_{|\bigcup\mathfrak{a}|},\,\beta\in\mathbf{S}_{|\bigcup\mathfrak{b}|}\end{subarray}}\{A\subset[N_{1}+N_{2}]|\;\mathbf{std}\left((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$})(A\cap\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$})\right)\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$},\mathbf{st}((\Lambda\square M)\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A\cap\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}}$})=\alpha,

\displaystyle\mathbf{std}\left((\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{L}$}\bullet\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$})(A\cap\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}^{\prime})\right)\geq\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$},\mathbf{st}((\Lambda\square M)\,\raisebox{-5.0pt}{$|_{A\cap\bigcup\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{M}$}^{\prime}}$})=\beta\}|.

using arguments similar to the proof of
Theorem

3.46
: indeed there exists unique
\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{a}$},\resizebox{}{655360}{$\mathfrak{b}$}\in\mathbf{IP}
and
\alpha,\beta
which “split”

\mathfrak{s}

and
\sigma
, respectively.
∎

.

Remark 4.22

(Arbitrary delays)
.

Since we count patterns, where two values can be either consecutive or have an arbitrary gap, a natural question might be whether it is possible to count patterns so that there is a specific time gap between values. This is indeed possible.

Consider, for example,
the task of counting the pattern
21
with
exactly

one gap between the two timepoints of the occurence.
pictorially, we can represent such a pattern as

5
Summary and outlook

In this work, we introduced two new Hopf algebras.
The Hopf algebra on interval partitions in
Section

3
encodes the
vincular
part of a permutation pattern.

This Hopf algebra can be equivalently seen as a Hopf algebra on words of positive integers where the filtered product
♠
possesses a shuffle part and the coproduct is deconcatenation, see
Remark

3.33
.
We define a family of linear functionals parametrized by interval partitions and show that they are characters and satisfy a Chen’s type identity.

The underlying combinatorics here is quite simple since the number of “occurrences” of one word into another is a closed-form expression that depends on the letters of the two words, see
Remark

3.36
.

Finally, in
Section

4
, we introduce the Hopf algebra on vincular patterns which is built upon our Hopf algebra on interval partitions and the superinfiltration Hopf algebra introduced in
[
15
]
. We also extend the definition of the functionals from
Section

3
to store the number of occurrences of vincular patterns. These maps are shown again to behave like
signatures
, satisfying identities which are reminiscent of the shuffle and the Chen’s identities for paths.

5.1
Open question

We are interested in the following open questions.

–

Is there a recursive definition for the product
♥
?

–

Both Hopf algebras,
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}},{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}},\Delta_{\bullet})
and
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}},{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}},\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}})
are free commutative as algebras, see
[
4
]
[Theorem 4.4.1]. Are there “interesting” sets of free commutative generators? An analogy we have in mind: the shuffle Hopf algebra is connected and graded and therefore automatically isomorphic, as an algebra, to a polynomial algebra. Though, one can also explicitly show that the shuffle algebra is a polynomial algebra over the set of Lyndon words.

–

Is the algebra on interval partitions
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}},{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}})
, or equivalently
(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Q}[\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}]^{\otimes n},\underset{\tiny\textup{wrd}}{{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}})
, isomorphic to the shuffle algebra
(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{Q}[\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}]^{\otimes n},\shuffle)
?

–

Since the Hopf algebras in this work are connected and filtered, one can compute the antipode using the well-known Takeuchi’s formula, see
[
14
]
[lemma 14], but cancellations can occur. Indeed, this happens in our case. If we compute the antipode in
\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box
on
\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}}
we obtain

\displaystyle\sum_{k\geq 0}(-1)^{k}{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}}^{k-1}\circ(\operatorname{id}-\eta\circ\varepsilon)\circ\Delta_{\bullet}^{k-1}(\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\quad 0-\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box+2\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box+2\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box+2\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\quad\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box+2\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box+2\;\Box\kern-1.1pt\Box

Are there cancellation-free formulas for the antipodes of our Hopf algebras?
In
[
12
]
, the authors provide a cancellation-free formula for the antipode of
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{per}},\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}},\Delta_{\square})
.

–

The Hopf algebra
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{vinc}},{\text{\color[rgb]{0.74,1,0.24}♥}},\Delta_{\resizebox{}{26214}{$\blacksquare$}})
“originates” from
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{int}},{{\text{\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}{♠}}}},\Delta_{\bullet})
and
(\mathcal{H}_{\tiny\textbf{per}},\raisebox{2.15277pt}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Rightarrow$}},\Delta_{\square})
. Is this an instance of a more general construction?

Appendix A
Gluing partitions is associative

The aim of this section is to show that the binary operation from
Definition

3.11
is associative.
We found it easier to formulate the operation
more abstractly first.
We will obtain the desired statement as
a special case,
Lemma

A.10
.

A.1
Assumptions

Let
\Omega
be a non-empty set
and consider maps

\displaystyle Q\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\Omega\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}

\displaystyle m\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\to\Omega.

We assume

P1.

\forall x\in\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(x,x)=1
,

P2.

\forall x,y\in\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(x,y)=1\implies Q(y,x)=1
,

P3.

\forall A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\forall y\in\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(m(A),y)=1\iff\exists x\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(x,y)=1
,

P4.

\forall A,B\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\>m(A\cup B)=m(\{m(A)\}\cup B)
.

Remark A.1
.

Let
A_{1},...,A_{n},B\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
. As a consequence of
4.
, one has

\displaystyle m(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\cup B)=m(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\{m(A_{i})\}\cup B)

A.2
Compression

Definition A.2

(Compression of
A
)
.

Let
\mathsf{compr}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\to 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
where

\displaystyle\mathsf{compr}(A)=\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})|x\in A\}

and
\sim_{A}
is the smallest equivalence relation on
A
which contains the relation
R\subset A\times A
defined as:

\displaystyle(x,y)\in R\iff Q(x,y)=1.

Before stating
Proposition

A.6
, we need three lemmas.

Lemma A.3
.

Let
A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
. Then

i.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(x,y)=1\implies[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}

ii.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1\iff[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}

iii.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(x,m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1\iff[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}

iv.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})=m([y]_{\sim_{A}})\iff[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}

v.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)}m([y]_{\sim_{A}})\iff m([x]_{\sim_{A}})=m([y]_{\sim_{A}})

Proof.

i
. follows from the definition of
\sim_{A}
.

ii
. We have

\displaystyle[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}\implies Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),m([x]_{\sim_{A}}))=1

by P1.
On the other hand

\displaystyle Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1

implies, P3,
\exists w\in[x]_{\sim_{A}}
such that
Q(w,m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1
which implies, P2 and P3,
\exists z\in[y]_{\sim_{A}}
such that
Q(w,z)=1
. Therefore
x\sim_{A}w\sim_{A}z\sim_{A}y
, i.e.
[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}
.

iii
.

If
Q(x,m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1

then, P3, there is
w\in[y]_{\sim_{A}}
such that
Q(x,w)=1
. Then
x\sim_{A}w\sim_{A}y
, i.e.
[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}
.

If
[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}
, then
Q(x,m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=Q(x,m([x]_{\sim_{A}}))=1
,
by P3, since
x\in[x]_{\sim_{A}}
.

iv
.
If
m([x]_{\sim_{A}})=m([y]_{\sim_{A}})
, then
Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1
and therefore, by ii.,
[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}
.
The other implication is immediate.

v
. Let
m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)}m([y]_{\sim_{A}})
, then
\exists w_{1},...,w_{n}\in A
such that

\displaystyle\forall i\in\{1,...,n-1\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}Q(m([w_{i}]_{\sim_{A}}),m([w_{i+1}]_{\sim_{A}}))=1

and
Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),w_{1})=1
and
Q(w_{n},m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1
. But then we have

\displaystyle m([x]_{\sim_{A}})=m([w_{1}]_{\sim_{A}})=\cdots=m([w_{n}]_{\sim_{A}})=m([y]_{\sim_{A}}).

∎

Lemma A.4
.

Let
A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
. Then

i.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A}y\iff x\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}y

ii.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A}y\iff m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}y

iii.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A}y\iff x\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}m([y]_{\sim_{A}})

iv.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A}y\iff m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}m([y]_{\sim_{A}})

v.

\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A}y\iff m([x]_{\sim_{A}})=m([y]_{\sim_{A}})

Proof.

These are consequences of properties P1, P2 and P3
and of the sets being equivalence classes and of the previous lemma.
∎

Lemma A.5
.

For
A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
,
x,y\in A
,

\displaystyle m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\in[y]_{\sim_{A}}\Rightarrow[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}

Proof.

Since
Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),m([y]_{\sim_{A}}))=1
, then
by
Lemma

A.3
ii.,
[x]_{\sim_{A}}=[y]_{\sim_{A}}
.
∎

The map
\mathsf{compr}
satisfies a form of idempotence.

Proposition A.6
.

For
A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
,

\displaystyle\mathsf{compr}(A)=\mathsf{compr}(\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A).

Proof.

We define the map

\displaystyle g\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\{[x]_{\sim_{A}}|x\in A\}

\displaystyle\to\{[z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}|z\in\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A\}

\displaystyle[x]_{\sim_{A}}

\displaystyle\mapsto[x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}

and show that it is surjective (one can show that it is also injective, with
Lemma

A.5
but we do not need this here). We need to show that

\displaystyle\{[x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}}\})|x\in A\}=\{[z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}|z\in\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A\}

Let
x\in A
, then

\displaystyle[x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}\subset[x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}.

Indeed, this follows from
Lemma

A.4

\displaystyle y\sim_{A}x\implies y\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}x

and, since
Q(m([x]_{\sim_{A}}),x)=1
, from
Lemma

A.3

\displaystyle m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}x.

For the other direction, let
w\in[x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}
and
w\in A
. Then, from
Lemma

A.4
, we know that
w\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}x
implies
w\sim_{A}x
, and
w\in[x]_{\sim_{A}}
. If
w\in[x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}
and
w\in\mathsf{compr}(A)
, we can write
w=m([u]_{\sim_{A}})
for some
u\in A
. Then, from the previous
Lemma

A.4
, we know that
m([u]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}x
, implies
[u]_{\sim_{A}}=[x]_{\sim_{A}}
, and
w=m([x]_{\sim_{A}})
. Therefore

\displaystyle[x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}=[x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}\in\{[z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}|z\in\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A\}.

Now let
z\in A
, we have

\displaystyle[z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}=[z]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([z]_{\sim_{A}})\}

and in case
z\in\mathsf{compr}(A)
, which means
z=m([u]_{\sim_{A}})
for some
u\in A
,

\displaystyle[z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}=[u]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([u]_{\sim_{A}})\}

using analogous arguments used to show the previous inclusion. This shows

\displaystyle g(\{[x]_{\sim_{A}}|x\in A\})=\{[x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}|x\in A\}=\{[z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}}|z\in\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A\}

If we use property 4 of
m
, we get the desired result

\displaystyle\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})|x\in A\}

\displaystyle=\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup[x]_{\sim_{A}})|x\in A\}

\displaystyle=\{m\left([x]_{\sim_{A}}\cup\{m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}\right)|x\in A\}

\displaystyle=\{m([z]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A}})|z\in\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup A\}.

∎

We now state a lemma used in the proof of the upcoming
Proposition

A.8
.

Lemma A.7
.

Let
A,B\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
. Then

\displaystyle\forall x,y\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A\cup B}y\iff m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([y]_{\sim_{A}})

\displaystyle\forall x\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\forall y\in B\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A\cup B}y\iff m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}y

\displaystyle\forall x,y\in B\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x\sim_{A\cup B}y\iff x\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}y

Proof.

These statements are similar to the ones of
Lemma

A.3
and
Lemma

A.4
, and the proof is also similar.
∎

We now show the main result.

Proposition A.8
.

Let
A,B\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
. Then

\displaystyle\mathsf{compr}(A\cup B)=\mathsf{compr}(\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B)

Proof.

Let
x\in A
. We can write

\displaystyle[m([x]_{\sim_{A}})]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}}

\displaystyle=\{u\in\mathsf{compr}(A)|u\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}\cup\{b\in B|b\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}.

We now show that

\displaystyle\{u\in\mathsf{compr}(A)|u\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}\}=\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})|a\in A,a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}.

Thanks to
Lemma

A.7
,
a\in A
such that
a\sim_{A\cup B}x
, implies
m([a]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})
. Therefore we have

\displaystyle\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})|a\in A,a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}

\displaystyle\subset\{u\in\mathsf{compr}(A)|u\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}.

Now let
u\in\{u\in\mathsf{compr}(A)|u\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}
, which means
u=m([z]_{\sim_{A}})
for some
z\in A
. Then we have

\displaystyle m([z]_{\sim_{A}})\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\implies z\sim_{A\cup B}x,

which means

\displaystyle m([z]_{\sim_{A}})\in\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})|a\in A,a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}.

Therefore

\displaystyle\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})|a\in A,a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}

\displaystyle\supset\{u\in\mathsf{compr}(A)|u\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}.

Similarly, we can also show that

\displaystyle\{b\in B|b\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}m([x]_{\sim_{A}})\}

\displaystyle=\{b\in B|b\sim_{A\cup B}x\}.

We can now finally write

\displaystyle m([m([x]_{\sim_{A}})]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}})

\displaystyle=m\left(\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})|a\in A,a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}\cup\{b\in B|b\sim_{A\cup B}\}\right)

(10)

We also obviously have

\displaystyle m([x]_{\sim_{A\cup B}})

\displaystyle=m\left(\{a\in A|a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}\cup\{b\in B|b\sim_{A\cup B}x\}\right)

(11)

We now show that
Equation

10
and
Equation

11
are equal. Notice that it is quite straightforward to verify that

\displaystyle\{a\in A|a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}=\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in A\\
a\sim_{A\cup B}x\end{subarray}}[a]_{\sim_{A}}

and using property 4 of
m
yields:

\displaystyle m\left(\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in A\\
a\sim_{A\cup B}x\end{subarray}}[a]_{\sim_{A}}\right)=m\left(\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in A\\
a\sim_{A\cup B}x\end{subarray}}\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})\}\right)=m\left(\{m([a]_{\sim_{A}})|a\in A,a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}\right)

and therefore

\displaystyle m([x]_{\sim_{A\cup B}})=m([m([x]_{\sim_{A}})]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}}).

(12)

Now let
x\in B
. We can write

\displaystyle[x]_{\sim_{A\cup B}}=\{a\in A|a\sim_{A\cup B}x\}\cup\{b\in B|b\sim_{A\cup B}x\}

and

\displaystyle[x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}}=\{y\in\mathsf{compr}(A)|y\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}x\}\cup\{b\in B|b\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}x\}

With steps similar to the ones used to show
Equation

12
, one obtains

\displaystyle m([x]_{\sim_{A\cup B}})=m([x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}}).

Since

\displaystyle\forall x\in A\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}m([x]_{\sim_{A\cup B}})

\displaystyle=m([m([x]_{\sim_{A}})]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}}),

\displaystyle\forall x\in B\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}m([x]_{\sim_{A\cup B}})

\displaystyle=m([x]_{\sim_{\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B}}),

we have shown that any element in
\mathsf{compr}(A\cup B)
can be written as an element of
\mathsf{compr}(\mathsf{compr}(A)\cup B)
and vice-versa, which finishes the proof.
∎

A.3
Associativity

Define
M\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\times 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\to 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
as

\displaystyle M(A,B)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathsf{compr}(A\cup B).

(2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\},M)
is a semigroup as illustrated in the following proposition.

Proposition A.9

(Associativity of M)
.

\displaystyle\forall A,B,C\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}M(A,M(B,C))=M(M(A,B),C)

Proof.

As a consequence of
Proposition

A.8
one has

\displaystyle\mathsf{compr}(A\cup\mathsf{compr}(B\cup C))=\mathsf{compr}(A\cup B\cup C)=\mathsf{compr}(\mathsf{compr}(A\cup B)\cup C)

∎

We are now ready to show that the operation
\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}
(see
Definition

3.11
) is associative.

Lemma A.10
.

Let
\mathcal{I},\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}
. Then:

\displaystyle(\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime})

Proof.

\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=2^{\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
,
and

\displaystyle\forall x,y\in\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\,Q(x,y)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if}\;x\cap y\neq\emptyset\\
0,&\text{else}\end{cases}

\displaystyle\forall A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\,m(A)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigcup_{x\in A}x

satisfy assumptions 1,2,3 and 4 from
Section

A.1
. Indeed,
2. follows from the commutativity of
\cap
,
1. follows from the idempotence of
\cap
,
3. follows by definition of union,
and regarding 4., for
A,B\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}

\displaystyle m\left(\{m(A)\}\cup B\right)

\displaystyle=m(\{\bigcup_{x\in A}x\}\cup B)

\displaystyle=m(\{\bigcup_{x\in A}x\}\cup\{y|y\in B\})

\displaystyle=\bigcup_{x\in A}x\cup\bigcup_{y\in B}y

\displaystyle=\bigcup_{z\in A\cup B}z

\displaystyle=m(A\cup B),

as claimed.

We hence get from
Proposition

A.9
that

\displaystyle M\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\times 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\to 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\}

is associative. Now from
Lemma

3.13
, it follows that, in particular,
\forall\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}\setminus\{\emptyset\}

\displaystyle M(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J})=\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{J}\in\mathbf{IP}\setminus\{\emptyset\}.

Therefore we can restrict and corestrict
M

\displaystyle M\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbf{IP}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\times\mathbf{IP}\setminus\{\emptyset\}\to\mathbf{IP}\setminus\{\emptyset\},

which is automatically associative. From
Definition

3.11
it follows immediately that
\forall\mathcal{I}\in\mathbf{IP}

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\emptyset=\mathcal{I}.

Therefore

\forall\mathcal{I},\mathcal{I}^{\prime},\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{IP}

\displaystyle(\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime})\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}=\mathcal{I}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}(\mathcal{I}^{\prime}\cdot_{\textbf{{glue}}}\mathcal{I}^{\prime\prime}).

∎

Remark A.11
.

Another example of
m
and
Q
satisfying the properties P1-P4 is as follows.
Let
\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}
and
set

\displaystyle\forall x,y\in\Omega,\;Q(x,y)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=1

\displaystyle\forall A\in 2^{\Omega}\setminus\{\emptyset\},\;m(A)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\max(A).

Properties P1-P3 are trivially satisfied since
Q
is always 1 and P4 obviously holds since

\displaystyle\max(A\cup B)

\displaystyle=\max(\{\max(A)\}\cup B).

Now let
\Omega\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{N}^{k}\setminus\{(0,\dots,0)\}
where
k>1
. Set

\displaystyle Q((x_{1},\dots,x_{k}),(y_{1},\dots,y_{k}))=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if}\;\;\exists i\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}x_{i}\neq 0\land y_{i}\neq 0\\
0,&\text{else}.\end{cases}

and

\displaystyle m(A)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=({\max}^{(1)}(A),\dots,{\max}^{(k)}(A))

where
\max^{(i)}(A)
is the maximum element of the i-th component of all the elements in
A
. One can show that P1-P4 hold also for this example.
